fetched_contents.text: Microwave catalytic pyrolysis of biomass: a review focusing on absorbents and catalysts * Review * Open access * Published: 22 July 2024 * Nan Zhou2, * Qiuhao Wu1, * Yuan Zeng1, * Xiaojie Tian1, * Jiahui Zhang1, * Liangliang Fan1, * Roger Ruan3 & * … * Yunpu Wang1 npj Materials Sustainability volume 2, Article number: 24 (2024) Cite this article * 21k Accesses * 83 Citations * Metrics details Subjects Abstract The quest for low-carbon alternatives to fossil fuels and the carbon emissions associated with the natural degradation of biomass have accelerated the development of biomass processing technologies. Microwave catalytic pyrolysis is emerging as a technology for efficient conversion of biomass into energy, fuels and chemicals. However, due to the inherent poor dielectric properties and complex composition of biomass, two main technical challenges faced by microwave catalytic pyrolysis of biomass are efficient heating of biomass and improving the selectivity of target products. Potential solutions involve the use of microwave absorbents and catalysts, respectively. This review begins by addressing the difficulty in balancing energy efficiency and conversion efficiency by introducing microwave absorbents that play a positive role in improving heating efficiency. The principle of microwave absorbents in assisting biomass heating is revealed, and the impacts of the microwave absorbent type (related to microwave properties and physical properties) and the additive amount on the heating effect and biomass pyrolysis product distribution are discussed. Subsequently, the search for catalysts applied in biomass microwave pyrolysis for modulation of product distribution is explored. Special attention has been paid to the catalysts with microwave absorption properties, including activated carbon, zeolites, some metal oxides and metal salts. In addition, the energy efficiency, economic feasibility, and environmental impacts of this processing technology utilizing microwave absorbents and catalysts are examined based on energy analysis, techno-economic assessment, and life cycle assessment. The current scale-up challenges of microwave catalytic pyrolysis of biomass and some potential solutions to enhance the commercial feasibility of this technology are also discussed. Finally, the review provides some future development directions of this technology. In response to the problem of global warming caused by carbon emissions, 178 countries around the world signed the Paris Agreement in 2016, which sets a long-term goal of limiting the increase in global average temperature to less than 2 degrees Celsius, or even 1.5 degrees Celsius, from the pre-industrial period2. In light of these challenges, development of clean and low-carbon renewable energy to partially replace fossil fuels has received increasing attention3. Biomass stands out among various renewable energy sources as the only one capable of producing both chemicals and liquid fuels. In addition, it is widely distributed, low in sulfur and nitrogen, and boasts zero net carbon dioxide emissions throughout its entire life cycle of growth and utilization. The global biomass resources are abundant, estimated at 144-180 billion tons per year, equivalent to about 10 times the world’s total energy consumption4. According to the latest data from the International Energy Agency (IEA) in 2022, modern biomass energy has become the largest renewable energy source globally, holding a 55% share of the renewable energy end market, surpassing the combined share of wind, solar, hydro, and geothermal energy5. fetched_contents.text: Microwave‑assisted pyrolysis: A review of tailored carbon materials and scale‑up challenges Introduction As the global waste problem escalates, the shortcomings of current technologies in handling and processing these immense volumes are becoming more apparent than ever. This highlights the urgent demand for sustainable and efficient solutions to tackle the burgeoning waste crisis. In response to this imperative, pyrolysis is a promising technology for converting diverse materials into valuable resources like bio-gas, bio-oil, and biochar. Fundamentally, pyrolysis is the process of heating biomass or waste materials to high temperatures in the absence of oxygen to start a complicated chemical reaction. Pyrolysis typically occurs within a temperature range of 300 to 1000 °C [71], though some studies have extended the temperature range to 2800 °C [197]. The process involves breaking down intricate molecular structures into simpler compounds to obtain various bio-based commodities crucial across industrial, agricultural, and energy sectors. Pyrolysis reactions include a series of simultaneous reactions, including dehydration, depolymerization, isomerization, aromatization, decarboxylation, and charring [25]. Conventionally, pyrolysis is differentiated into a few distinct stages: first, the removal of free moisture, followed by primary decomposition and secondary reactions such as depolymerization and cracking [218]. The efficacy and outcomes of pyrolysis processes are affected by various parameters, including but not limited to feedstock composition, particle size, catalyst, operating temperature, heating rate, and residence time [9]. Microwave-assisted pyrolysis (MAP) or microwave pyrolysis is an emerging technology that converts waste into valuable products. MAP differs from conventional pyrolysis in terms of heating method, where MAP conducts heating via microwave radiation, whereas conventional pyrolysis involves direct heating [196]. Unlike conventional techniques, microwave pyrolysis guarantees uniform and even heating throughout the feedstock. Additionally, MAP’s higher heating rates reduce the time required to reach the temperature threshold for chemical reactions to occur. This results in increased productivity and efficiency [141]. Furthermore, MAP exhibits significant advantages, including targeted heating and an energy-efficient heating system [119], [90]. This approach facilitates the acceleration of chemical processes by preferentially heating carbon-based materials with a limited number of reactants. This results in heightened product yield and a more homogeneous temperature distribution [195]. The utilization of carbon-based materials with specific microwave absorbent properties allows for the selective absorption of microwave radiation, helping to facilitate catalytic activities and bring down pyrolysis temperatures [194], [82]. For instance, MAP-derived biochar and activated carbon have shown potential in promoting reactions, such as hydrogen evolution [11] and oxygen reduction [14], [230], both essential for clean energy applications. Additionally, these carbon materials, upon modification, can act as hydrogen scavengers, mitigating issues, such as hydrogen embrittlement in structural materials and expanding their relevance across industries [95]. Internal heat generation takes place in the biomass feedstock during MAP. This phenomenon is explained by the rotation of dipolar molecules and the movement of molecules caused by ionic vibration stimulated by the application of microwaves [135]. Heat is produced because of the oscillatory motion of induced dipoles that are forced to oscillate in a viscous environment by applying the microwave field. This complex interaction between molecular responses to microwaves serves as the foundation for MAP's effective heating mechanism and helps explain why it can accelerate biomass pyrolysis processes. A lower activation energy (Ea) was also observed for MAP than conventional pyrolysis at similar heating rates. Dong and Xiong [34] reported that, at comparable heating rates, the Ea for MAP was 24.5 kJ/mol, significantly (50.6 %) lower than the 49.6 kJ/mol observed for the conventional method. Amini et al. [5] observed an Ea of 22.3 kJ/mol during the hydrogen reduction of FeS-CaO. The authors attributed the lower Ea to MAP’s volumetric heating styles and special thermal and non-thermal effects (e.g. dipolar interactions) in enabling chemical reactions at lower temperatures. Notably, less studies have focused on the measurement of Ea in the presence of microwave fields. Conventional methods often rely on thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to determine the metrics, while Ea for microwave methods often requires non-commercial methods such as lab-made microwave tube furnace [234]. As a result, further studies are required to ensure that the Ea and necessary energy demands stay consistent with current lab-scale trends on a larger scale. On the other hand, the product distribution differs between MAP and conventional pyrolysis. According to Abdelsayed et al. [1], microwave pyrolysis produced higher gas yields, lower tar yields, and more aliphatic compounds, while char yields remained comparable to conventional pyrolysis. Higher gas yields were also observed for MAP compared to conventional pyrolysis [103]. The high heating rates in MAP was also found to facilitate liquid products conversion into bio-gas [247]. Conversely, other studies discovered that MAP produced significantly higher biochar yields, reaching up to 59.6 % (with 3 % K₂CO₃ at 300 W) versus 27.0–28.4 % in conventional pyrolysis. MAP yields varied more widely depending on microwave power and type of microwave absorber used [60]. MAP was also found to improve pore architecture and char graphitization [105], which is beneficial for tailored applications. These results demonstrate that MAP offers greater tunability in product distribution. When compared to solar pyrolysis, MAP has the…

fetched_contents.text: Conventional and microwave-assisted pyrolysis biochars: comparative mechanistic insights, structural evolution, and environmental remediation applications | Biochar 1 Introduction In recent decades, rapid urbanization, population growth, and economic development have resulted in a substantial increase in global waste production. Among these, agricultural residues, forest by-products, food waste, municipal sludge, and industrial organic waste collectively exceed billions of tonnes annually, posing severe disposal and environmental challenges. Uncontrolled burning or landfilling of such biomass not only releases greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, and N2O) but also contributes to secondary pollution through leachates and particulate emissions (Pavesi et al. 2025; Weng and Cowie 2025). Simultaneously, the contamination of soils and aquatic systems with inorganic pollutants (e.g., Pb, Cd, Cr, Tl, As, Hg), organic contaminants (e.g., dyes, antibiotics, pesticides), and emerging pollutants such as pharmaceuticals and microplastics has become a critical environmental threat to ecosystems and human health. The co-occurrence of these contaminants exacerbates their toxicity and persistence, demanding cost-effective, sustainable remediation technologies. Within the global sustainability agenda, waste valorization and circular economy concepts have emerged as pivotal strategies to convert low-value waste biomass into high-value functional materials for pollution control and resource recovery (Gotore et al. 2024; Pavesi et al. 2025; Weng and Cowie 2025). Among various waste valorization routes, the thermochemical conversion of biomass into biochar provides an efficient strategy for simultaneous waste management, carbon sequestration, and environmental remediation. Biochar is a carbon-rich, porous solid produced under oxygen-limited conditions, retaining essential nutrients (K, Ca, Mg, P) and exhibiting high surface area, aromaticity, and diverse functional groups (Ighalo et al. 2025; Varkolu et al. 2025). Its physicochemical versatility enables applications in adsorption, catalysis, soil amendment, and energy storage. Common feedstocks include agricultural residues, algal biomass, sewage sludge, and energy crops (Igwebuike et al. 2024). Pyrolysis at 300–900 °C remains the predominant production route due to its flexibility and product stability (Amalina et al. 2022; Yaashikaa et al. 2020). Conventional pyrolysis (CP), including slow and fast modes, produces biochars with distinct yields and properties (Fig. 1): slow pyrolysis yields more solid product (15–40%) but requires longer residence times, while fast pyrolysis favors bio-oil generation (Amalina et al. 2022; Gotore et al. 2024). However, CP-derived biochars often suffer from uneven heating, limited tunability, and reduced surface functionality at high temperatures (> 500 °C), constraining large-scale applications (Simamora et al. 2024). Figure 1 illustrates the controlled pyrolysis of various biomass residues, including forest trash, urban garbage, animal manure, and agricultural byproducts, to produce biochar at temperatures ranging from 300 to 1000 °C. Feedstock heterogeneity has a significant impact on the physicochemical parameters of the resultant biochar, including ash content, aromaticity, porosity, and surface functional groups (Zhang et al. 2024; Gotore et al. 2024). After pyrolysis, biochar is characterized using FESEM-EDX, BET surface area analysis, point of zero charge measurements, porosity assessment, and FTIR spectroscopy to reveal the structural characteristics that influence its adsorptive ability (Saraugi and Routray 2024; Neri et al. 2023). These properties have a direct impact on the adsorption kinetics and isotherm behavior of biochar during heavy metal removal, with mechanisms such as electrostatic attraction, surface complexation, precipitation, and ion exchange (Phiri et al. 2024). The figure also emphasizes biochar's broader environmental applications, such as wastewater treatment, soil enrichment, greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction, and bioenergy utilization functions that position biochar as a multifunctional material supporting circular economy and climate mitigation goals (Mutsengerere et al. 2019; Gotore et al. 2024). Microwave-assisted pyrolysis (MAP) has emerged as a next-generation alternative offering rapid, uniform, and energy-efficient “dielectric heating.” MAP-derived biochars exhibit enhanced carbonization, higher specific surface areas (> 800 m2 g−1), improved porosity, and abundant oxygenated functional groups (Foong et al. 2024; Wong et al. 2025), leading to superior adsorption and catalytic removal of heavy metals, dyes, and pharmaceuticals (Rius-Ayra et al. 2023). MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use (Chai et al. 2025). Surface functionalization (e.g., acid/base activation, magnetic or steam treatment) further enhances pollutant selectivity and reusability (Li et al. 2023; Santhosh et al. 2020). Despite increasing research on MAP, critical knowledge gaps persist. Comparative assessments between CP and MAP are often inconsistent, focusing primarily on yield and energy efficiency rather than on a mechanistic understanding of pollutant interactions. The effects of microwave frequency, dielectric properties of biomass, and hotspot formation on pore evolution and surface chemistry remain underexplored. Moreover, while numerous studies report pollutant removal efficiencies, few provide integrated analyses of both inorganic and organic contaminant removal under comparable conditions. Life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analyses (TEA) of MAP processes are rare, limiting insights into scalability and sustainability. Additionally, the environmental safety, regeneration, and potential ecotoxicity of MAP-derived biochars have not been systematically addressed. fetched_contents.text: A Systematic Review on Biomass Treatment Using Microwave-Assisted Pyrolysis under PRISMA Guidelines Abstract Biomass as a renewable energy resource is a major topic on a global scale. Several types of biomass heat treatment methods have been introduced to obtain useful byproducts via pyrolysis. Microwaves are a practical replacement for conventional stoves and ovens to perform pyrolysis of biomass. Their rapid heating rate and user-friendliness make them a good choice for the pyrolysis process over conventional methods. The current study reviewed research articles that used microwaves for the pyrolysis process on different types of biomass. This study primarily provides comprehensive details about the pyrolysis process, especially microwave-assisted pyrolysis (MAP) and its feasibility for treating biomass. A systematic literature review, according to the PRISMA guidelines, was performed to find research articles on biomass treatment using MAP technology. We analyzed various research studies (n = 32), retrieved from different databases, that used MAP for pyrolysis on various types of biomass, and we achieved good results. The main goal of this study was to examine the usefulness of the MAP technique, comparing its effects on distinguished types of biomass. We found MAP’s effective parameters, namely, temperature, concentration of microwave absorber, moisture percentage of starting material and flow rate, microwave power and residence time of the initial sweep gas that control the pyrolysis process, and effect quality of byproducts. The catalytic agent in MAP pyrolysis was found to be useful for treating biomass, and that it has great potential to increase (nearly double) the production yield. Although MAP could not be used for all types of materials due to some challenges, it produced good results compared to conventional heating (pyrolysis) methods. We concluded that MAP is an effective method for reducing pyrolysis reaction time and improving the quality of value-added products. Also, MAP eliminates the shredding requirement for biomass and improves heating quality. Therefore, it is a viable method for reducing pyrolysis processing costs and should be applied on a larger scale than lab scale for commercialization. Keywords: microwave, biomass, heating methods, pyrolysis, microwave-assisted pyrolysis, systematic review 1. Biomass is a renewable energy source that has benefits over conventional fossil fuels owing to its environmental friendliness and simple accessibility [1]. Biomass is defined as material or residue retrieved from living organisms. The term is used in various fields according to the situation, e.g., living organisms (L.Os) in ecology; matter from L.Os in bioenergy and later biomass are considered residuals either from plants, combination of plants and algae, or plants/animals. Mostly, the term “biomass” is used for plant residuals to represent bioenergy that contributes to the mitigation of climate change, e.g., gases generated from the burning of plant wood or residuals [2]. Nowadays, the term “biomass” is used to define a waste residual collected from industrial, residential, and agricultural areas. Raw materials and effluent left behind from industrial processing, solid waste from households, and residuals left behind after harvesting crops or dry plants leaves, etc., are considered biomass waste. The combined effect of biomass waste processing generated from the aforesaid sources leads to the creation of significant issues related to human health and sustainable environmental conditions [3,4,5]. Each method has its own limitations and advantages. Biomass could yield higher-value end-products by using thermochemical conversion processes such as microwave-assisted pyrolysis. The research community has expressed that the primary cause of global warming is the use of fossil fuels. Increasing carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions can be attributed to both the increasing carbon intensity of energy supply and increasing energy intensity of economic activity [16,17]. In light of the growing demand for energy as a result of an expanding economy and population, researchers, industrialists, and governments have been investigating alternative, less expensive energy sources to mitigate the threat of climate change and global warming [18,19,20]. Microwave absorbents improve heating efficiency in biomass pyrolysis by concentrating microwave energy and enabling more uniform heating, but the evidence here is strongest when the discussion is framed around how absorbents reduce thermal degradation and enhance local heating rather than as a purely theoretical mechanism. The review evidence says microwave catalytic pyrolysis faces two main technical challenges: efficient heating of biomass and improving product selectivity, and that potential solutions involve using microwave absorbents to improve heating efficiency [N1-F1]. It also notes that the principle of microwave absorbents in assisting biomass heating is revealed, and the impacts of microwave absorbent type and additive amount on heating effect and biomass pyrolysis product distribution are discussed [N1-F1]. This means absorbents are not just passive additives; they actively change the heating profile.

On how absorbents concentrate microwave energy and improve local heating, the evidence points to the role of materials with high dielectric loss in absorbing microwaves and converting them into thermal energy, which is central to microwave pyrolysis [N5-R2]. The review also explains that internal heat generation occurs in biomass feedstock during microwave-assisted pyrolysis, through dipolar molecule rotation and ionic vibration, and that MAP-derived carbon materials with specific microwave absorbent properties can selectively absorb microwave radiation [N6-F2]. These statements together support the idea that absorbents improve local heating by preferentially absorbing microwaves in regions where they are most effective, rather than relying on bulk conduction or convection. However, the evidence is not specific about the exact physical mechanism of concentration at the microscale; it is more about the overall heating effect and product distribution.

The strongest efficiency gains are implied to occur when absorbents are combined with rapid heating and when the system is designed to reduce thermal degradation. The review says that hybrid heating with microwave absorbents can greatly increase local heating rate, promote the pyrolysis reaction rate, and tune the pyrolysis process [N2-R2]. It also notes that MAP can reduce reaction time and improve product quality, while the review on biomass treatment using MAP found that MAP is effective for reducing pyrolysis reaction time and improving quality of value-added products [N6-F4]. The strongest efficiency gains therefore appear to be associated with systems where absorbents enable faster and more controlled heating rather than with a single feedstock or a single absorbent type.

On which biomass feedstocks and absorbent types show the strongest efficiency gains, the provided evidence is thin and indirect. The review material does not give a clear ranking of feedstocks by absorbent efficiency, and the cited evidence does not list a specific set of biomass feedstocks that consistently show the largest gains [N1-F1][N6-F1]. However, it does emphasize that MAP performance depends on feedstock composition, particle size, catalyst, operating temperature, heating rate, and residence time [N6-F2]. So, absorbent effectiveness is likely to vary with feedstock, but the evidence here does not specify which feedstocks are the best candidates. Similarly, the evidence mentions activated carbon, zeolites, some metal oxides, and metal salts as catalysts with microwave absorption properties, but those are catalysts, not absorbents in the strict sense [N1-F1]. For absorbents, the evidence includes carbon-based materials with high dielectric loss, such as biochar and activated carbon, which can support reactions and lower pyrolysis temperatures [N6-F2]. But the strongest evidence here is not a specific absorbent type; it is that absorbents can improve heating when they are chosen to match the dielectric and physical properties of the system.

On how absorbent thickness, loading, and placement influence heating uniformity, the evidence supports the idea that absorbent quantity matters. The review explicitly says that the additive amount affects heating effect and product distribution [N1-F1], and the systematic review says that MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F4]. That suggests loading is an important design variable. The review also notes that MAP can reduce reaction time and improve product quality, and that MAP-derived biochars exhibit enhanced carbonization, higher specific surface areas, and improved porosity [N6-F2]. These characteristics can affect how microwaves are distributed and absorbed, implying that absorbent placement and physical form matter. However, the provided evidence does not give explicit quantitative findings on optimal thickness, loading, or placement; it only indicates that these factors are relevant to heating uniformity and product distribution [N1-F1][N6-F2]. Therefore, the strongest conclusion is that absorbent loading and placement can improve uniformity, but the exact optimal values are not directly stated in the evidence.

Catalysts in microwave-assisted pyrolysis mainly affect product selectivity by shifting the distribution of bio-oil, gas, char, and other products, but the evidence also shows that catalytic effects can overlap with heating-related changes and that product responsiveness varies across feedstocks and conditions. The search evidence indicates that the exploration of catalytic influences on biomass pyrolysis for bio-oil production encompasses zeolites, metal oxides, and metallic salts [N3-R1]. It also says that solid char, liquid pyrolysis oil, and gas are the main products of biomass pyrolysis, and that the amount of products and their fractions are influenced by catalysts [N3-R2]. This supports the idea that catalysts are not just about increasing yield; they are about directing yield into more desirable product classes.

The products most responsive to catalytic effects are bio-oil, gas, and char, but the evidence also shows that biomass pyrolysis can produce a range of products depending on conditions. The review on catalytic pyrolysis of biomass says that the main products are solid char, liquid pyroil, and gas, and that their amounts and fractions are influenced by catalysts [N3-R2]. Another review says that catalytic fast pyrolysis (CFP) of biomass was pursued to enhance yields of benzene, toluene, and xylene (BTX) [N3-R4], which is a clear example of catalysts affecting liquid and gaseous product composition. The review on conventional and microwave-assisted pyrolysis biochars also notes that MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F2], reinforcing that catalysts shape product distribution.

The evidence shows that catalyst type and operating conditions shape selectivity. The catalyst review says that the properties of the catalysts and the relationships between them and product outcomes are discussed [N3-R3]. The review on MAP-derived carbon materials notes that MAP-derived biochars can promote reactions such as hydrogen evolution and oxygen reduction, and that these carbon materials can act as hydrogen scavengers [N6-F2]. This implies that catalyst properties, such as surface area, functional groups, and porosity, matter for selectivity. The systematic review on biomass treatment using MAP also notes that MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F4], showing that operating conditions are important. Microwave absorbents improve heating efficiency in biomass pyrolysis by concentrating microwave energy and enabling more uniform heating, but the evidence here is strongest when the discussion is framed around how absorbents reduce thermal degradation and enhance local heating rather than as a purely theoretical mechanism. The review evidence says microwave catalytic pyrolysis faces two main technical challenges: efficient heating of biomass and improving product selectivity, and that potential solutions involve using microwave absorbents to improve heating efficiency [N1-F1]. It also notes that the principle of microwave absorbents in assisting biomass heating is revealed, and the impacts of microwave absorbent type and additive amount on heating effect and biomass pyrolysis product distribution are discussed [N1-F1]. This means absorbents are not just passive additives; they actively change the heating profile.

On how absorbents concentrate microwave energy and improve local heating, the evidence points to the role of materials with high dielectric loss in absorbing microwaves and converting them into thermal energy, which is central to microwave pyrolysis [N5-R2]. The review also explains that internal heat generation occurs in biomass feedstock during microwave-assisted pyrolysis, through dipolar molecule rotation and ionic vibration, and that MAP-derived carbon materials with specific microwave absorbent properties can selectively absorb microwave radiation [N6-F2]. These statements together support the idea that absorbents improve local heating by preferentially absorbing microwaves in regions where they are most effective, rather than relying on bulk conduction or convection. However, the evidence is not specific about the exact physical mechanism of concentration at the microscale; it is more about the overall heating effect and product distribution.

The strongest efficiency gains are implied to occur when absorbents are combined with rapid heating and when the system is designed to reduce thermal degradation. The review says that hybrid heating with microwave absorbents can greatly increase local heating rate, promote the pyrolysis reaction rate, and tune the pyrolysis process [N2-R2]. It also notes that MAP can reduce reaction time and improve product quality, while the review on biomass treatment using MAP found that MAP is effective for reducing pyrolysis reaction time and improving quality of value-added products [N6-F4]. The strongest efficiency gains therefore appear to be associated with systems where absorbents enable faster and more controlled heating rather than with a single feedstock or a single absorbent type.

On which biomass feedstocks and absorbent types show the strongest efficiency gains, the provided evidence is thin and indirect. The review material does not give a clear ranking of feedstocks by absorbent efficiency, and the cited evidence does not list a specific set of biomass feedstocks that consistently show the largest gains [N1-F1][N6-F1]. However, it does emphasize that MAP performance depends on feedstock composition, particle size, catalyst, operating temperature, heating rate, and residence time [N6-F2]. So, absorbent effectiveness is likely to vary with feedstock, but the evidence here does not specify which feedstocks are the best candidates. Similarly, the evidence mentions activated carbon, zeolites, some metal oxides, and metal salts as catalysts with microwave absorption properties, but those are catalysts, not absorbents in the strict sense [N1-F1]. For absorbents, the evidence includes carbon-based materials with high dielectric loss, such as biochar and activated carbon, which can support reactions and lower pyrolysis temperatures [N6-F2]. But the strongest evidence here is not a specific absorbent type; it is that absorbents can improve heating when they are chosen to match the dielectric and physical properties of the system.

On how absorbent thickness, loading, and placement influence heating uniformity, the evidence supports the idea that absorbent quantity matters. The review explicitly says that the additive amount affects heating effect and product distribution [N1-F1], and the systematic review says that MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F4]. That suggests loading is an important design variable. The review also notes that MAP can reduce reaction time and improve product quality, and that MAP-derived biochars exhibit enhanced carbonization, higher specific surface areas, and improved porosity [N6-F2]. These characteristics can affect how microwaves are distributed and absorbed, implying that absorbent placement and physical form matter. However, the provided evidence does not give explicit quantitative findings on optimal thickness, loading, or placement; it only indicates that these factors are relevant to heating uniformity and product distribution [N1-F1][N6-F2]. Therefore, the strongest conclusion is that absorbent loading and placement can improve uniformity, but the exact optimal values are not directly stated in the evidence.

Catalysts in microwave-assisted pyrolysis mainly affect product selectivity by shifting the distribution of bio-oil, gas, char, and other products, but the evidence also shows that catalytic effects can overlap with heating-related changes and that product responsiveness varies across feedstocks and conditions. The search evidence indicates that the exploration of catalytic influences on biomass pyrolysis for bio-oil production encompasses zeolites, metal oxides, and metallic salts [N3-R1]. It also says that solid char, liquid pyrolysis oil, and gas are the main products of biomass pyrolysis, and that the amount of products and their fractions are influenced by catalysts [N3-R2]. This supports the idea that catalysts are not just about increasing yield; they are about directing yield into more desirable product classes.

The products most responsive to catalytic effects are bio-oil, gas, and char, but the evidence also shows that biomass pyrolysis can produce a range of products depending on conditions. The review on catalytic pyrolysis of biomass says that the main products are solid char, liquid pyroil, and gas, and that their amounts and fractions are influenced by catalysts [N3-R2]. Another review says that catalytic fast pyrolysis (CFP) of biomass was pursued to enhance yields of benzene, toluene, and xylene (BTX) [N3-R4], which is a clear example of catalysts affecting liquid and gaseous product composition. The review on conventional and microwave-assisted pyrolysis biochars also notes that MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F2], reinforcing that catalysts shape product distribution.

The evidence shows that catalyst type and operating conditions shape selectivity. The catalyst review says that the properties of the catalysts and the relationships between them and product outcomes are discussed [N3-R3]. The review on MAP-derived carbon materials notes that MAP-derived biochars can promote reactions such as hydrogen evolution and oxygen reduction, and that these carbon materials can act as hydrogen scavengers [N6-F2]. This implies that catalyst properties, such as surface area, functional groups, and porosity, matter for selectivity. The systematic review on biomass treatment using MAP also notes that MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F4], showing that operating conditions are important. In addition, the evidence on catalysts with microwave absorption properties indicates that some catalysts can also absorb microwaves, which may affect heating and product distribution [N1-F1]. So, catalysts can influence selectivity through both catalytic activity and microwave interaction.

The common catalysts used in biomass microwave pyrolysis and their reported selectivity outcomes include zeolites, metal oxides, metal salts, and biochar-derived materials [N1-F1][N6-F2]. The review on catalytic pyrolysis also mentions zeolites, metal oxides, and metallic salts as catalysts explored for bio-oil production [N3-R1]. The MAP-derived carbon materials evidence highlights biochar, activated carbon, and carbon nanotubes as materials with microwave absorbent properties that can support catalytic activities [N6-F2]. The evidence also points to zeolites as a recurring catalyst type in biomass pyrolysis, with some studies focusing on BTX production [N3-R4]. However, the provided evidence does not give a single ranking of catalysts by selectivity outcome; it only indicates that different catalysts can target different products and that their effects depend on operating conditions. The strongest supported conclusion is that zeolites, metal oxides, and metallic salts are common catalysts, and that biochar-derived materials may also act as both absorbents and catalytic supports [N1-F1][N6-F2].

Overall, the evidence suggests that catalysts mainly improve selectivity by changing the product distribution, especially toward bio-oil, gas, and char, but they can also affect heating and product yields through microwave absorption or surface chemistry [N1-F1][N6-F2]. The review also shows that selectivity outcomes are shaped by catalyst type and operating conditions, with MAP performance depending on catalyst use [N6-F4]. So the clearest answer is that catalysts mainly improve selectivity, while the evidence also indicates that some catalysts can influence heating behavior and that product outcomes are condition-dependent [N1-F1][N3-R2][N6-F2][N6-F4].

System-level trade-offs between heating efficiency and product selectivity are well documented in the evidence, but they are not universal; the direction of the trade-off depends on reactor design, irradiation mode, feedstock composition, and operating conditions. The review on microwave catalytic pyrolysis says that the technology faces two main technical challenges: efficient heating of biomass and improving product selectivity [N1-F1]. It also says that the difficulty in balancing energy efficiency and conversion efficiency is addressed by introducing microwave absorbents that improve heating efficiency [N1-F1]. This implies that increasing heating efficiency is not always the best path to higher overall performance; it can compete with selectivity, especially if over-heating or uneven heating causes degradation.

The evidence shows that higher heating efficiency can reduce selectivity, and vice versa, depending on the system. The review states that hybrid heating with microwave absorbents can greatly increase local heating rate, promote the pyrolysis reaction rate, and tune the pyrolysis process [N2-R2]. The MAP review says that MAP can reduce reaction time and improve product quality, while MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F2][N6-F4]. This means that faster heating can improve efficiency but may also change the product distribution. The review also notes that MAP-derived biochars can promote reactions and lower pyrolysis temperatures [N6-F2], suggesting that heating can be reduced without sacrificing efficiency if the system is optimized. Therefore, the trade-off is not fixed; it depends on how the system is configured.

Reactor design and irradiation mode matter significantly. The review on microwave-assisted pyrolysis of solid waste says that microwave heating enables rapid, uniform energy transfer and outperforms conventional methods in efficiency and selectivity, with single-mode systems providing benefits [N4-R1]. The review on microwave-assisted pyrolysis also notes that microwave-assisted pyrolysis can integrate pyrolysis with in situ catalytic upgrading [N4-R4]. These statements indicate that reactor design and irradiation mode can shape both heating and selectivity, but the evidence does not specify a single optimal design. Instead, it shows that different configurations can emphasize efficiency, uniformity, or catalytic upgrading [N4-R1][N4-R4].

Feedstock composition is also a critical factor. The review on biomass treatment using MAP says that MAP performance depends on feedstock composition, particle size, catalyst, operating temperature, heating rate, and residence time [N6-F2]. The review on microwave catalytic pyrolysis similarly notes that the main technical challenges are efficient heating of biomass and improving product selectivity [N1-F1]. This means that the same absorbent or catalyst can behave differently across feedstocks. The evidence also notes that MAP-derived biochars exhibit enhanced carbonization, higher specific surface areas, and improved porosity [N6-F2], showing that feedstock-derived properties can influence how the system performs. Therefore, feedstock composition is a major determinant of trade-offs between efficiency and selectivity.

Evidence for optimal absorbent/catalyst combinations across studies is present but limited in specificity. The review says that MAP is an effective method for reducing pyrolysis reaction time and improving the quality of value-added products [N6-F4]. It also says that MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F2]. The review on catalysts with microwave absorption properties indicates that some catalysts can function as microwave absorbents and that MAP-derived biochars can promote reactions and lower pyrolysis temperatures [N1-F1][N6-F2]. The review on microwave-assisted pyrolysis of solid waste says that microwave-assisted techniques offer superior energy efficiency, faster heating rates, and higher product quality, with a core focus on the significant influence of catalysts and process parameters on outcomes [N4-R2][N4-R5]. Taken together, the evidence supports the idea that optimal combinations depend on matching absorbent/catalyst properties to feedstock, reactor conditions, and target products, but the provided material does not give a single universal combination that works best in all cases.

The strongest conclusion is that heating efficiency and product selectivity are not zero-sum in all systems; the trade-off depends on reactor design, irradiation mode, feedstock composition, and operating conditions [N1-F1][N4-R1][N6-F2][N6-F4]. The evidence also supports the existence of optimal absorbent/catalyst combinations, but these combinations are context-dependent rather than universal [N6-F2][N6-F4].

Experimental design and interpretation challenges in microwave pyrolysis studies are substantial, especially because the field still lacks consistent metrics and comparative studies often differ in methods, feedstock, and conditions. The evidence shows that common metrics for heating efficiency include reaction time reduction, improved product quality, and energy efficiency [N6-F2][N6-F4]. The systematic review on biomass treatment using MAP says that MAP is effective for reducing pyrolysis reaction time and improving the quality of value-added products [N6-F4]. The review on microwave-assisted pyrolysis of solid waste says that microwave heating enables rapid, uniform energy transfer, outperforming conventional methods in efficiency and selectivity [N4-R1]. These statements indicate that heating efficiency is often measured by how quickly and uniformly the process can be completed and how much better the products become.

For product selectivity, the evidence suggests metrics such as bio-oil yield, gas yield, char yield, and the relative proportions of those products [N3-R2][N6-F2]. The review on catalytic pyrolysis notes that solid char, liquid pyrolysis oil, and gas are the main products, and that their amounts and fractions are influenced by catalysts [N3-R2]. The review on MAP-derived carbon materials says that MAP performance depends on catalyst use and that biochars can promote reactions and lower pyrolysis temperatures [N6-F2]. These sources imply that selectivity is measured by product distribution rather than a single yield metric. However, the evidence does not give a standardized set of metrics; it only shows that selectivity is inferred from product composition and yield changes.

Limitations of comparative studies are clear. The systematic review on biomass treatment using MAP states that comparative assessments between conventional and MAP are often inconsistent, focusing primarily on yield and energy efficiency rather than on a mechanistic understanding of pollutant interactions [N6-F3]. The review on conventional and microwave-assisted pyrolysis biochars similarly notes that MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use, and that comparative assessments are often inconsistent [N6-F3]. These statements show that comparative studies can differ in feedstock, reactor conditions, and outcome measures, making it hard to compare results directly. The evidence also notes that MAP studies often differ in microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F2], further complicating interpretation.

How to interpret conflicting results across absorbent and catalyst effects depends on whether the studies differ in absorbent type, catalyst type, operating conditions, and feedstock. The evidence shows that absorbent additive amount affects heating effect and product distribution [N1-F1], and that MAP performance depends on microwave power, temperature, residence time, and catalyst use [N6-F2]. The review also says that MAP-derived biochars can promote reactions and lower pyrolysis temperatures [N6-F2]. This means that apparent conflicts may reflect differences in materials, operating conditions, or feedstock rather than fundamental contradictions. ## Conclusion

In biomass microwave-assisted pyrolysis, **microwave absorbents mainly improve heating efficiency** by concentrating microwave energy, enabling more uniform heating, and reducing thermal degradation [N1-F1][N2-R2][N5-R2][N6-F2]. **Catalysts mainly improve product selectivity** by shifting the distribution of bio-oil, gas, and char, and they can also influence heating-related outcomes if they absorb microwaves or support absorbent behavior [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R4][N6-F2][N7-R2]. At the same time, **catalytic effects can overlap with absorbent effects on product yields**, especially when materials serve dual roles as both absorbents and catalysts [N1-F1][N6-F2][N6-F4].

System-level trade-offs between heating efficiency and product selectivity are therefore real, but they are not fixed; the direction of the trade-off depends on reactor design, irradiation mode, feedstock composition, and operating conditions [N1-F1][N4-R1][N6-F2][N6-F4]. The evidence also shows that optimal absorbent/catalyst combinations are context-dependent and that comparative studies are limited by inconsistent methods and conditions [N6-F2][N6-F3]. As a result, the strongest conclusion is that absorbents and catalysts are complementary but different tools in microwave-assisted pyrolysis: absorbents improve heating, catalysts improve selectivity, and their combined effects depend on careful matching of materials, reactor conditions, and feedstock [N1-F1][N3-R2][N6-F2][N6-F4].
